newsitem.title: GERMANY: Many Germans fearful of euro, survey finds.
newsitem.headline: Many Germans fearful of euro, survey finds.

text.p: Almost half the German population is fearful of Europe's planned single currency because of worries the euro will be worth less than their German mark, an opinion survey published on Thursday found.
The respected Wickert Institute said that 47 percent of 870 adults surveyed were frightened by the proposed single currency while 53 percent said they were not concerned.

Those fearing the economic and monetary union (EMU) listed the following reasons: the euro would be a "devalued" currency (51 percent), "purchasing power would be diminished" (15 percent) and the project "lacks transparency" (13 percent).

Other reasons cited for their worries about the euro included: "lower quality of life", the EMU is "moving forward too quickly and mistakes are thus unavoidable", and there are too many "different cultures and mentalities" in Europe.
Most of those who were not afraid of the euro said "things would work out in the end" (26 percent) and it could "no longer be stopped" (24 percent).
The study by the Tuebingen-based institute also found that 58 percent felt insufficiently informed by the media about the euro compared to 42 percent saying they had obtained enough information.
